newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian ex-PM ends campaign in historic square.
newsitem.headline: Romanian ex-PM ends campaign in historic square.

text.p: Former prime minister Petre Roman closed his presidential campaign on Wednesday with an impassioned plea to vote out incumbent Ion Iliescu -- delivered on the spot where both men led the 1989 anti-communist revolt.

Opinion polls say Roman, the country's first post-communist prime minister, is in third place in Sunday's increasingly tight presidential race behind Iliescu, a former communist, and academic Emil Constantinescu.
Roman told 5,000 supporters that Revolution Square, where megalomaniac dictator Nicolae Ceausescu last appeared in public before his capture and execution,was a sacred place for him.

"I was there on that balcony, shortly after the dictator's flight. I had the chance to speak to the crowds of people I had come with on the streets on Bucharest," Roman said, gesturing at the former Communist Party headquarters.
"On December 22, 1989, I felt the day of freedom had come. We no longer felt afraid. That's how I feel today. Don't be afraid...Iliescu's regime will fall!"
Roman spoke to seething crowds in 1989 from the balcony of the party headquarters, now the upper house of parliament, after Ceausescu had fled aboard a helicopter.
Iliescu also appeared on the same balcony that day and told crowds: "Comrades, now's the time to build real socialism". He then took the lead by announcing Ceausescu's fall on state television.
Roman, the author of Romania's initial market reforms, worked in tandem for a while with Iliescu, who has been in power since the 1989 upheaval.
But he was forced from office after coal miners denouncing austerity measures ransacked Bucharest in September 1991. He has since said the miners acted at Iliescu's behest.
Opinion surveys credit Iliescu, who portrays himself as a bulwark of stability, with a three to four point lead over Constantinescu. A run-off vote will almost certainly be required later this month.
All 16 candidates, including a faith healer, leaders of a car drivers' and pensioners party and two rival socialists, will take part in a 3-1/2 hour television debate on Thursday.

In parliamentary elections also being held on Sunday, Iliescu's ruling Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) trails Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR), a bloc of 15 parties. Tough coalition talks are likely to follow the polls.
Iliescu told a television interviewer he regretted the split with Roman two years after they had worked together within a National Salvation Front (FSN) to overthrow dictatorship.

"The FSN leadership split because of the temptation to grab power," he said on private ProTV. "We have wasted two years in fostering reforms because of tensions associated with the split and a guerrilla-like fight between the two wings."

Roman and Constantinescu dismiss the president as a vestige of a communist system yet to be fully revamped. They have focused on plunging living standards which have left millions of Romanians in poverty with average monthly wages below $100, one third the level in Poland.

"We know that Iliescu has condoned the corruption and dishonesty spread across this country," Roman told a packed indoor rally earlier. "This is the legacy of his regime. This is what we have to topple on November 3." REUTER
